Move w64devkit.ini to the root to mirror "installs"

One of my goals is that the distribution can be re-built in place using
only Docker or Podman, and so the unpacked distribution mirrors the
repository layout. That hasn't been true for w64devkit.ini, which is the
only file interfering with this trick, so fix it.

Use ftpmirror.gnu.org for downloads

llvm-mingw switched to using it in this commit:
https://github.com/mstorsjo/llvm-mingw/commit/a96bbc0c

And I figured we should do the same. Especially since we download more
than just GNU make.

GNU themselves write (https://www.gnu.org/server/mirror.en.html):

> We recommend using this generic ftpmirror.gnu.org address wherever
> possible in links, documentation, etc., to reduce load on the main GNU
> server.

Build and include widl tool from Mingw-w64

The widl configure script is broken and does not support out-of-source
builds, so unlike gendef just above, it's built in the source tree. The
--prefix and --with-widl-includedir options must be congruent despite
their artificiality. These two paths are combined to construct the real
sysroot path at run time via tools.h:build_relative_path.

This patch also creates arch-prefixed aliases for both gendef and widl.
Don't specify gmp, mpfr, mpc include and lib directories separately

make: Disable "fast" path pseudo-shell

When a build command is sufficiently simple, GNU Make simulates a shell
("fast") instead of starting a real shell ("slow"). This simulation is

and so on. The "fast" path does not appear to be faster, so rather than
fix it just disable it with a small patch.

cmake: normalize breakpoint paths

The breakpoint manager normalizes incoming setBreakpoints paths with
GetActualCaseForPath, but SourceFileLoaded and GetBreakpoints use
paths from CollapseFullPath, which preserves whatever case the caller
provided.  On case-insensitive filesystems these can differ for the
same file, so the unordered_map keys do not match and breakpoints are
silently missed.

On macOS (HFS+) GetActualCaseForPath is a no-op, so the setBreakpoints
path passes through unmodified.  If the DAP client sends "Test.cmake"
but cmake was invoked with "cmake -P test.cmake", the breakpoint is
stored under "Test.cmake" while GetBreakpoints looks up "test.cmake".

On Windows GetActualCaseForPath *does* normalize, but only in
HandleSetBreakpointsRequest.  The breakpoint is stored under the
canonical "Test.cmake", while SourceFileLoaded and GetBreakpoints
still receive "test.cmake" from CollapseFullPath.  The keys disagree
from the opposite direction.

Add a NormalizePath helper and apply it in all three public entry
points so that every map key goes through the same transformation.
On non-Windows it uses GetRealPath (wrapping realpath(3), which
returns the actual filesystem case on macOS and resolves symlinks on
Linux).  On Windows the existing GetActualCaseForPath is retained.

ninja: Fix deps log recovery

In DepsLog::Load(), the file offset used for truncation-based recovery
was advanced past each record immediately after reading its bytes from
disk, but before validating the record's semantic correctness (e.g. the
path checksum or node-id range checks). When a record was structurally
complete but semantically invalid, recovery truncated the file to an
offset that included the bad record, so it was never removed.

This created an infinite cycle: every build would load the deps log, hit
the corrupt record, "recover" by truncating everything after it (but not
the record itself), then append new dependency records that would be
destroyed by the next build's recovery. The result was spurious rebuilds
on every invocation.

Move the offset update to the end of the loop body, after all validation
has passed. Now when a record fails validation, the offset still points
before it, and truncation correctly removes it.

(This patch has been submitted upstream.)

Upgrade to GCC 16.1.0

Bumps GCC from 15.2.0 and adjusts the build for the new release:

- Drop the obsolete stdcall-align patch, no longer needed.

- Configure with --enable-tls so libstdc++ uses native Windows TLS
  rather than emutls. This is an ABI break: object files built with
  earlier w64devkit releases cannot be linked against new builds.

- Import gcc-dynamic-load-tzdb.patch (originally from
  redpanda-cpp/mingw-lite, by CyanoHao) so that libstdc++'s C++20
  std::chrono::current_zone() Windows backend resolves
  GetDynamicTimeZoneInformation at runtime via LoadLibrary/
  GetProcAddress. Without this, _WIN32_WINNT < 0x0600 builds fail
  to compile tzdb.cc.

- Add gcc-libgfortran-mapview.patch to replace the new
  MapViewOfFileExNuma call in libgfortran's caf_shmem with
  MapViewOfFileEx, which mingw-w64 declares for older Windows
  targets. NUMA_NO_PREFERRED_NODE makes the two calls equivalent,
  so no functional change.

Switch code-signing to aas-sign

Replace the windows-latest sign job (azure/login + azure/artifact-
signing-action) with a single Linux release job that uses
skeeto/aas-sign@v1.0.0. aas-sign handles the GitHub OIDC -> Azure
exchange directly, so the Azure CLI step is no longer needed and the
signed-artifact handoff to a separate release job collapses into one
step.

Also align the draft logic with sibling projects (dcmake, elfeed2,
stackcalc): tags vX.Y.Z-rcN are pipeline-test runs published as draft
prereleases; tags vX.Y.Z publish immediately.

Move code-signing into the build pipeline

Sign every PE inside the toolchain (~250 .exe and .dll), pack, then
sign the resulting self-extracting archive. All signing runs at
docker run time so the bulk of the build remains fully cacheable
and secrets never enter image layers.

Stage layout:
- dl-aas-sign / build-aas-sign: SHA-pinned source tarball with
  vendored mbedtls + nlohmann/json, built with the base image's
  Debian gcc.
- final: assembly only (drop the trailing 7z + CMD).
- signed (new): COPY aas-sign + sign-and-pack.sh, CMD runs the
  script at docker run time. Reads AZURE_CLIENT_ID/TENANT_ID and
  the GitHub OIDC env vars from -e flags.
- pack (new, default target): RUN 7z + CMD cat sfx archive.
  Behaviorally identical to the old final.

The release workflow rebuilds --target signed for each arch
(reusing the same GHA cache scope as the unsigned pack build),
then docker runs the image to produce the signed package on
stdout.

Add NSIS 3.12 (makensis only)

Adds a CLI-only NSIS install for compiling .nsi scripts. Skips the
GUI wizards (makensisw, the NSIS installer creator) and documentation.

Path-resolution problem: makensis at $PREFIX/bin/makensis.exe would
auto-detect NSISDIR=$PREFIX (parent dir of bin), so NSIS would look
for $PREFIX/{Include,Stubs,Plugins,...} -- collides with w64devkit's
own $PREFIX/include on Windows's case-insensitive filesystem. Solve
by installing the real makensis under $PREFIX/share/nsis/bin/, where
auto-detection lands correctly on $PREFIX/share/nsis. A small alias
EXE at $PREFIX/bin/makensis.exe (built from the existing alias.c)
exec's it. Fully relocatable, no env vars.

New stages: dl-nsis, build-nsis. SCons + python3 only inside
build-nsis (not base) to avoid cache invalidation. TARGET_ARCH
derived from $ARCH at build time so the same Dockerfile works for
x64 and x86 -- no variant-x86.patch hunk needed.

contrib: Add bootstrap-go-toolchain.sh

Ever since w64devkit began forcing bigobj by default, it has been
incompatible with cgo. I patched go to support bigobj, but unfortunately
upstream the patch ran in to bureaucracy/difficulties and I ran out of
patience to get it through. So that means it's not really an option to
use upstream go binaries, it must build from source. Bootstrapping go is
not difficult, but it has grown more tedious as more required stages
have been added to the bootstrap chain.

So, to spare myself some tedium, I have created
bootstrap-go-toolchain.sh. It builds the latest version of go, from
source, using only w64devkit's gcc compiler. It also adds my bigobj
patches to the toolchain, so cgo works properly.

ci: fix non-release version stripping; gate source.tar on tags

Two issues with non-release builds:

* git describe --always falls back to a commit SHA (e.g. abc123) on
  branches without a recent tag. The old ${GIT_VERSION:1} stripped
  the first character unconditionally -- fine for v2.8.0 -> 2.8.0,
  but produced bc123 from a SHA. Use ${GIT_VERSION#v} instead so the
  v is removed only when present.

* source.tar is a release artifact, not a CI artifact -- the source
  Docker target build, the tar extraction, and the artifact upload
  were running on every push. Gate the three steps on
  startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/') so non-release builds skip
  them entirely.

gcc: Patch undefined handle_contract_violation #393

libstdc++exp.a's default handle_contract_violation is marked weak so
users can supply their own. PE-COFF __attribute__((weak)) does not act
as an ELF-style fallback definition; it makes the symbol an alias for
some other (strong) definition. With no such definition the default
never resolves and -fcontracts -lstdc++exp fails to link.

Drop the weak attribute so the default is an ordinary strong symbol.

crt: __MINGW_IMP_SYMBOL for _strtof_l and _wcstof_l

These functions are static emulations present in every libmsvcr*.a,
but the headers declare them dllimport (_CRTIMP), so callers reference
__imp__strtof_l and __imp__wcstof_l, which nothing defines, and the
link fails. Define fake import pointers alongside the definitions, as
already done for other statically-emulated functions such as
__acrt_iob_func and _initialize_onexit_table.

The _strtof_l half was merged upstream after v14.0.0 as 373c7dd0
("crt: Add missing __MINGW_IMP_SYMBOL for _strtof_l()"). The
_wcstof_l half is the same fix for the wide variant, which remains
broken upstream.

Fixes for ccache output on Windows consoles

Ccache captures compiler diagnostics and writes them to the terminal
itself. Its Unix-style isatty and TERM checks do not reliably describe
Win32 console capabilities, and its byte-oriented output path cannot
preserve Unicode outside the active code page.

The color bug can be reproduced in a legacy console without virtual
terminal processing:

    printf 'int main(void) { return undeclared; }\n' > error.c
    TERM=cygwin ccache gcc -c error.c

The diagnostic contains literal escape sequences such as ?[01m?[K
instead of colored text.

The Unicode bug can be reproduced with a non-ASCII identifier:

    printf 'float π(void) { return 3; }\nvoid f(void) { float unused = π(); }\n' > unicode.c
    ccache gcc -Wall -Wextra -c unicode.c
    ccache gcc -Wall -Wextra -c unicode.c

The source line emitted by ccache renders π as mojibake on both captured
and cached diagnostic output.

Add two ccache patches. The first detects native console handles with
GetConsoleMode, enables virtual terminal processing when available, and
otherwise translates supported SGR and erase-line sequences with Win32
console APIs. Redirected output remains unchanged.

The second decodes valid UTF-8 and writes non-ASCII text to native
consoles with WriteConsoleW. ASCII, invalid UTF-8, and redirected output
retain the existing byte-oriented path.

Apply both patches when building ccache.

Fixes skeeto/w64devkit#413.

Upgrade to ccache 4.14

- Windows path rewriting is now case-insensitive and Unicode-aware, and
  ignore_headers_in_manifest matches case-insensitively on Windows.
- Detects C23 #embed directives and assembler .incbin directives,
  preventing false cache hits.
- Removed the cpp_extension (CCACHE_EXTENSION) option; preprocessor
  output is now processed in memory instead of via temporary files.
- Fixed a size overflow when allocating very large files on Windows.

Both Windows console output patches were regenerated against 4.14.

for subprograms, because as and ld live in bin/ rather than a tooldir.
Invoked by absolute path, the toolchain no longer needs its bin/ in

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Fetch sources with ADD --checksum instead of curl

BuildKit keys ADD --checksum on the checksum and the URL basename, not
on the host, so re-pointing a download at another mirror is a cache hit
and does not even resolve the host. Swapping mirrors during an ftp.gnu.org
outage no longer costs a re-download of everything, which is the trap
that made the recent debian:trixie-slim digest bump so expensive.

Stages that fetched several tarballs in one curl now get one ADD each,
so a mirror change re-fetches a single file rather than all of dl-cross.

Names come from ADD's dest where the URL basename differs, replacing
curl --remote-header-name. This matters beyond cosmetics: every stage's
/dl/*.* is copied into /source/, so these names ship in the source
distribution. GitHub archive refs are the four affected downloads.

ADD cannot run a shell, so expat's tag gains an EXPAT_TAG arg rather
than deriving it from EXPAT_VERSION with tr.

Drops curl from base. BuildKit verifies TLS with its own trust store,
so the downloads are now authenticated rather than passing --insecure.

Add x86 multilib toolchain support

libraries, and winpthreads for both the bootstrap and final sysroots so
each compiler stage has a complete i686 runtime.

that defaults _WIN32_WINNT to 0x0501 only under -m32 and only when the
caller has not supplied a value, preserving the existing x64 default and
explicit overrides.

Retain the x86_64-w64-mingw32-prefixed tools and add a separate build
step for an i686-w64-mingw32 interface. Compiler drivers inject -m32.
Target-sensitive binutils select their 32-bit modes explicitly: as uses
--32, ld uses -m i386pe, dlltool uses -m i386 with --as-flags=--32, and
windres uses --target=pe-i386. Input-driven inspection and archive tools
forward without a target override.

These forwarding executables provide both prefixed interfaces without
duplicating a second binutils installation. They deliberately remain
selectors for the underlying x86_64-configured multilib compiler rather
than spoofing its configured target identity.

Replace the variant patch with Dockerfile build args

Hoist every variant-sensitive value into an ARG at the top of the cross
stage, with defaults producing the x64 kit, and gate the multilib-only
sidecar builds on MULTILIB. The x86 variant becomes a set of NAME=value
overrides in src/variant-x86.args, which multibuild.sh turns into
--build-arg options. A plain "docker build" continues to work untouched,
downloads stay shared between variants, and the patch mechanism remains
available as a fallback for a future variant needing structural changes.

One hazard of this approach: ARGs leak into the environment of every
subsequent RUN in the stage, and configure scripts read arbitrary
environment variables. mingw-w64-crt decides whether to build the Win64
runtime by testing whether a shell variable named LIB64 is merely set,
so an ARG of that name forced lib64 on past an explicit --disable-lib64.
Hence CRT_LIB64. Keep ARG names clear of names configure might consult.

Namespace the CMake profile flags

CMAKE_C_FLAGS and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS are real CMake variable names, and
profile values sit in the environment of every RUN, including the other
cmake invocations that do not pass these flags explicitly. CMake does
not read them from the environment today, but it honors a growing list
of CMAKE_* environment variables, so real names are a latent hazard.
Rename them and document the naming discipline alongside the profiles,
which also covers why CRT_LIB32/CRT_LIB64 avoid their obvious names.

Ship x86 NSIS stubs in the multilib kit

makensis is retargetable: the architecture of the installers it emits
is decided by which precompiled stub it attaches, stubs and plugins
are stored under target-suffixed names, and a script selects one with
"Target x86-unicode" (or CPU x86). Its default remains amd64, chosen
by the bitness of makensis itself. Add a second stub-and-plugin pass
so the multilib kit can emit 32-bit installers, which remain the
traditional choice even for 64-bit payloads since they run on every
Windows and can fail politely on 32-bit hosts.

The NSIS build derives each tool from XGCC_W32_PREFIX and never adds
-m32 on its own, so present the multilib compiler through an i686
interface: wrapper scripts that forward with -m32, --32, and
--target=pe-i386, mirroring the aliases the kit itself ships. The
x86-ansi extras come along unconditionally, matching the standalone
x86 kit's layout.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Manage patch queues with quilt series files

Move each component's patches from flat, prefixed file names into a
per-component directory with a quilt series file, dropping the number
prefixes: application order is now stated by series rather than
enforced by lexicographic glob expansion. Outside the build, a queue
is managed by our own quilt against an unpacked tarball from source/
with QUILT_PATCHES=/path/to/src/<component>. The shipped kit carries
the same layout under $W64DEVKIT_HOME/src, consumable by the bundled
quilt.exe the same way.

Inside the build, apply queues with Debian's original quilt rather
than a native build of src/quilt.cpp, whose amalgamation is
Windows-only. This keeps battle-tested GNU patch as the engine, and
makes every image build a conformance check: series semantics mean
whatever the reference implementation says, and a queue our clone
manages must be accepted by original quilt. The .pc state is removed
after each push because source trees are never popped, and a stale
.pc from one queue blocks pushing a second queue onto the same tree,
which happens twice: gcc then crossgcc, mingw then gendef.

Rename the crossgcc patch queue to gcc-final

"crossgcc" names a property both GCC builds share: /x-gcc is a plain
cross build and /gcc is a Canadian cross, so "cross" does not tell them
apart, and it points at the bootstrap compiler, which is the one queue
it does not apply to.

What separates the queues is reach. Both push onto the same tree, which
is never popped: src/gcc goes on before the bootstrap compiler and is
still applied when the shipped compiler configures, so it reaches both.
The second queue goes on top afterward and reaches only the compiler
that ships. Name it for that.

As a bonus the directories now sort in push order; crossgcc sorted
before gcc while being applied after it.
